The Frenchman will no longer be required to serve a one-match suspension after a ruling by an independent panel. He fouled Alexander Isak when the Liverpool forward was through on goal in the early stages at Anfield but Mauricio Pochettino, United’s new head coach, insisted the striker would not have reached the ball, and therefore was not a sending-off offence. The referee Sam Barrott made a different assessment, for which the video assistant referee did not seek a review, a judgment supported by Pro Ref’s chief refereeing officer, Webb.
“The reason we’re talking about it is the fourth consideration [in Dogso decisions], that’s control or likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball,” Webb told Mic’d Up, which was recorded before the confirmation of the card being annulled.
“Isak’s got control of the ball, he’s got possession, he’s got the touch, he knocks it past Yoro. He’s moving at pace at that moment, and a foul comes in and knocks him down. There’s a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get on to that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.
“I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. [It’s] certainly not clearly wrong.”
Pochettino expressed his opinion on Sunday: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”
Dominik Szoboszlai scored the resulting free-kick, setting Liverpool on their way to victory, to make it a difficult first match in charge for Pochettino. Yoro will now be available to face Brentford on Saturday in the Premier League.

Manchester United defender Leny Yoro has had the red card shown to him at Anfield overturned by the Football Association - even though referees' chief Howard Webb has backed the decision to send the defender off.
Yoro was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott for bringing down Liverpool forward Alexander Isak just eight minutes into Sunday's match.
Isak had run onto a ball that bounced over Matthijs de Ligt but took a heavy touch that meant the ball was likely to run through to United goalkeeper Senne Lammens even if Yoro had not brought down the Swede.
New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino was furious at a decision he felt had changed the course of the game, which Liverpool won 4-0.
"The ball wasn't in his control," he said. "Isak, when he saw the control wasn't good, it's normal to delay, and stop to the run. In that moment that Yoro came from the back, and you go down.
"But all that we play football; you know that wasn't intentional. That is never a foul."
The FA backed that view, meaning Yoro will be clear to face Brentford in the Premier League at Old Trafford on Saturday.
However, in the latest edition of Mic'd Up on Sky Sports, Webb said Barrott got it right.
"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball," he said.
'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?
How on earth can the head of referees say a decision was right, but the FA say it was wrong?
"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable," Webb said. "Certainly not clearly wrong."
Not clearly and obviously wrong for a VAR intervention, but clearly and obviously wrong for the FA to rescind the red card.
You wonder how the general fan is supposed to understand it all.
The FA's appeals process is notoriously difficult to predict, especially on highly borderline situations like Yoro.
A commission features three people, usually former players though sometimes there is a retired official is on the panel.
A simple majority is needed, so a club just needs two people to agree with them.
It's why clubs might appeal against red cards when it seems impossible to win, you just never know.
Such was the split of opinion on Yoro, United always stood a chance of at least getting those key two votes.
And this is the crux of appeals process. An FA commission is just the subjective opinion of three people.
Do the appeal again tomorrow with three different panel members, and United might lose.
This is why Pro Ref don't use the outcome of FA appeals to determine how games are officiated.
Two years ago, Brentford's Christian Norgaard won an appeal against a red card at Everton. That was a split 2:1 vote, but enough to say a decision was wrong.
Pro Ref told its referees not to alter their interpretation based on this vote.
Let's throw in another one. The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.
Earlier this season, Brighton appealed against Pascal Struijk's VAR red card at Sunderland.
An FA commission upheld the appeal, but in contradiction the KMI Panel voted the VAR intervention was correct.
This will forever be the problem with officiating, and indeed any hope of true consistency with VAR.
Was Yoro's red card right or wrong? On which side of the fence will the KMI Panel fall?
Football is just a floating mass of subjectivity. Of referees, of VARs, of panel members and of fans. It just depends whose opinion you ask.
Sporting coach Paulo Fonseca speaks to the media ahead of the Champions League clash with Manchester United
United have travelled to Lisbon for their next Champions League match on Wednesday (20:00 GMT).
The early dismissal of Yoro at Anfield meant Sporting had no chance to assess any changes Pochettino might have made after he replaced Michael Carrick during the international break.
But despite United sitting 19th in the Premier League, Sporting boss refuses to accept United are "fragile".
"I don't following the reasoning," said Fonseca, who was only appointed on 4 November after the Portuguese club bought him out of his contract at Lyon.
"Manchester is a great team," he said. "I don't believe a lot that great teams are fragile. The last game they played in the Champions League, they were trailing 2-0, then won 3-2 against a very difficult opponent in Roma.
"Moreover, when they have a new head coach, with such world-class players, it's extremely unpredictable to see if they will have a good day or bad day."
United have not won in the Premier League since August and have conceded 19 goals in their past six games in all competitions.
Yet, such was the nature of the Liverpool game, Fonseca has had to watch analysis of Pochettino's time in charge of the United States to get an idea of what to expect.
"Eight minutes, red card. It's impossible to make an analysis," he said.
"I tried to see Pochettino with the United States and what kind of solutions he used. There is some information but it is very difficult to predict."

Scottish striker Kirsty Howat signed for Crystal Palace in September 2025
Crystal Palace have been deducted three points after using too many substitution windows during their win on the opening day of the 2026-27 Women's Super League season.
Palace, who were playing their first match following promotion back to the WSL, beat Everton 1-0 on 6 September at Gander Green Lane.
However, manager Jo Potter brought on Kirsty Howat for Shannon O'Brien in the seventh minute of second-half stoppage time to try and shore up the victory.
It was the fourth separate substitution made by Potter, who had also made changes in the 62nd, 83rd and 90th minutes.
While WSL managers are allowed to make five changes in a game, they must be made across only three stoppages in play to avoid excessive time wasting.
Palace have been stripped of the three points they earned in the match - one of only two WSL games the Eagles have won this season.
This punishment drops Palace down one place in the WSL table to 13th - the relegation play-off place.
Palace are now below fellow promoted side Birmingham City in the table on goal difference, with both sides now having six points - six behind Everton in 11th.
In a statement on their club website , external Palace said they were "disappointed" by the decision.
The decision was made by an independent tribunal after Palace admitted the breach of competition rule 5.19.1.
The rule states: "A substitution can only be made when play is stopped for any reason and the referee has given permission. A club at its discretion may use five substitute players during a match. For the avoidance of doubt, each club has no more than three substitution opportunities in each match."
The tribunal said that while the rule breach was inadvertent and "not intended to secure an unfair advantage", it said a points deduction was necessary in order to provide a deterrent to clubs against making a similar mistake in future.
"The integrity of the competition would be damaged if a club that had breached the rules on substitution opportunities, and had won the match, were allowed to keep the points it obtained, save in exceptional circumstances," the tribunal stated in its full written decision. , external
They said the lateness of the substitution in the match - so late that Howat did not touch the ball after coming on - did not excuse Palace from punishment.
It also ruled "that responsibility for complying with the rule rests with clubs, not match officials".
Palace - who placed the word "fourth" in inverted commas in their response to the ruling - are aiming to improve on their only previous WSL campaign in 2024-25, where they only won twice in 22 matches and were relegated by a 10-point margin.
Their statement read: "Everyone at the club is obviously frustrated that such a minor infraction, given that the player was on the pitch for only 46 seconds while the ball was in play, has led to such a significant penalty – a penalty which we do not agree is reasonable or proportionate.
"We are disappointed for the players and staff who worked so hard to secure a deserved victory on our return to the WSL."
Forward Lexi Lloyd-Smith had scored the only goal of the game in the 34th minute on her Palace debut.

Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven is open to a loan move in January amid concerns over his game time as his side battles in the Premier League relegation zone.
The 20-year-old centre-back is concerned about what United's current situation means for his development, after new manager Mauricio Pochettino left him as an unused substitute in Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool .
Now on his third manager in 21 months since joining from Arsenal in February 2025, Heaven accepts Pochettino may prefer more experienced options as United attempt to avoid a shock relegation.
The club have also been heavily linked with signing a centre-back in the coming January window, with targets said to include Fulham 's Calvin Bassey.
However, the Cottagers regard Bassey as an important player and would not encourage any interest.
Fulham and Barcelona are among the clubs to have expressed an interest in Heaven, with both having tried to sign him when he decided to leave Arsenal .
The England U20s defender's preference is believed to be a loan move, though he would also entertain permanent offers.
At United he has largely been used as a back-up option and, after enjoying a run in the team under former manager Ruben Amorim, he lost his place under Michael Carrick. He returned to the side only after an injury crisis hit the club last season.
Heaven is also capable of playing at left-back and in midfield, but does not expect to be trusted as a regular starter amid the instability at Old Trafford, with the club 19th in the league.
He is under contract until 2029 in a deal that includes an option for an extra year.

In the latest edition of Match Officials Mic'd Up , Pro Ref chief refereeing officer Howard Webb analyses Man Utd defender Leny Yoro's sending off vs Liverpool - now overturned on appeal - as audio of how the officials handled the incident in real time is revealed
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Referees' chief Howard Webb has backed the process of the officials who sent off Manchester United defender Leny Yoro at Liverpool - despite the red card being overturned on appeal.
Yoro, sent off after eight minutes of Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Anfield , was due to face a one-match ban for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity when he brought down Alexander Isak outside the box and he was in on goal.
However, United have had the suspension lifted after a successful claim of wrongful dismissal, the FA said on Tuesday. The independent commission will publish the written reasons in "due course".
Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol: “I've looked back at past decisions of these commissions to see the make-up of the panel. "In the case of Brentford striker Igor Thiago - who was sent off for elbowing an opponent against Brighton earlier this month - the panel was made up of two former players in Tony Agana and Francis Benali, and a former referee, Steve Bennett.”
In the latest edition of Match Officials Mic'd Up, Webb, chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref, described the on-field decision from referee Samuel Barrott as "decisive" and said the point of contention was around whether Isak would beat United goalkeeper Senne Lammens to the ball.
Audio from the officials reveals that the VAR John Brooks, who backed Barrott's decision, determined Isak was "likely" to get on the end of the ball before Lammens. His assistant VAR, Paul Howard, agreed.
Webb was non-committal in his verdict but backed the process of the officials by saying "most people would see that as a correct decision".
"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens," said Webb. "Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. That was the referee's call made on the field.
"The VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect and formed the opinion that it wasn't. If there was any doubt, then it was doubt.
"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. And I think by and large most people would see that as a correct decision with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.
"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong."
REF - Sam Barrott: DOGSO (Denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity), DOGSO.
REF: Outside and it's a red card for DOGSO. On-field decision is outside, red card for DOGSO.
VAR - John Brooks: Checking the on-field decision of DOGSO. Longer loop, please.
VAR: Yeah, point of contact. Go 18 [yard] now, go 18. Clearly outside. First contact, clearly outside.
VAR: So, Isak is the right side, defender is the wrong side. Defender bundles into him, into the back. Gets too tight. I think it's a foul. Go back to 18-yard. Let's roll it through, firstly to see whether the attacker is going to get on the end of the ball. Just roll it through, real speed.
VAR: So, at full speed, Isak maintains his momentum and likely gets on the end of it. Certainly not clearly wrong that he doesn't. So I think the DOGSO is confirmed. We'll just check APP (Attacking Possession Phase).
VAR: Sam [referee], the DOGSO location and sanction is confirmed. Just checking the rest of the APP.
VAR: Yeah: Frame two, clearly onside. We've seen it all. Doesn't control the ball with the arm or anything, yes. Sam, confirming the on-field decision of a free-kick to Liverpool just outside the box and a denial of a goalscoring opportunity.
"Firstly, I think this was a really decisive decision by the referee Sam Barrott. We know it is clearly a foul and we also know it is outside the penalty area.
"We're thinking about the sanction. Is it a denial of an obvious goal scoring opportunity? There's actually four considerations officials have to think about.
"Direction of play: he is definitely going towards the goal. It's not going out wide. Proximity from goal: it's just outside the penalty area.
"The location of other defenders: there's only Yoro there. The keeper is moving back towards his own goal. He has to put the brakes on and possibly come back out.
"The reason we're talking about it is the fourth consideration. That's control or likelihood of keeping on or gaining control of the ball. Isak's got control of the ball. He's got possession. He's got the touch. He knocks it past Yoro. He's moving at pace at that moment. And a foul comes in and knocks him down.
"And there's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. That was the referee's call made on the field.
Former Premier League official Dermot Gallagher said it was the right call to show Yoro a red card on the latest edition of Ref Watch.
He said: "If you look at it from the referee's angle. Is it a foul? That's the first step. Yeah. Is he in possession of the ball? From that angle, yes. I think most people would've expected a red card. It would've been a surprise during the game if a red card hadn't been given.
"I don't know [if he would've gotten to the ball before Lammens]. You watch it play out. That happens. Do you think it's a red card? Gary Neville's immediate reaction was red card."

Crystal Palace have been deducted three points in the Women’s Super League after they made substitutions in four separate windows during their 1-0 victory over Everton in September.
Palace admitted breaching the competition’s rules and an independent tribunal ordered the points deduction, but no points will be awarded to Everton. It means Palace drop from 12th to 13th, below Birmingham City on goal difference. The match will not be replayed.
Palace made the substitutions during the second half and their 97th-minute introduction of Kirsty Howat, to replace Shannon O’Brien, was a breach of the rules. Teams have a maximum of three substitution windows per game, excluding half-time.
The WSL, Pro Ref and both clubs launched investigations. Promoted Palace led the opening-weekend game thanks to Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s 34th-minute goal and there were eight minutes of stoppage time indicated at the end.
The match officials who worked on the game were not appointed to any matches for the following round in the WSL and WSL2 in light of the incident.
The independent tribunal concluded Palace’s breach was inadvertent and that they had not tried to secure an unfair advantage. None of the parties involved are eligible to appeal.
Palace said: “Everyone at the club is obviously frustrated that such a minor infraction, given that the player was on the pitch for only 46 seconds while the ball was in play, has led to such a significant penalty – a penalty which we do not agree is reasonable or proportionate. We are disappointed for the players and staff who worked so hard to secure a deserved victory on our return to the WSL.”
Everton are also understood to be disappointed with the outcome but it is understood the club were not formally represented during the tribunal because the case was “The WSL versus Crystal Palace”. Everton wrote a letter to the tribunal which outlined their opinion that the introduction of Howat had a sporting impact.
Everton’s letter mentioned that they had accumulated seven shots after the 90th minute and 72% possession in stoppage time, indicating “that Everton were dominant and on top, chasing an equaliser” when the substitution broke the flow.
The Palace head coach, Jo Potter, told the tribunal that her assistant had suggested making the substitution.
The operations match manager’s report, submitted to the tribunal, stated the fourth official had not recorded Palace’s third substitution window in her notes because, when that was taking place in about the 90th minute, she was “simultaneously dealing with requests from the broadcast match manager, protests from both teams regarding decisions and added time, and the requirement to configure the added time for display on the fourth official’s board”.
Palace sit five points above the WSL’s automatic relegation place, having dropped from nine points to six. The side who finish 13th will play a relegation/promotion playoff against a WSL2 club.

Millwall, who are 16th in the Championship, have average league gates of 19,418 at The Den this season
Millwall have been ordered to play a future Championship match in front of a partially-closed stadium as punishment for fans' discriminatory chants.
The club has also been fined £70,000 by an independent regulatory commission, and been told another offence this season will lead to a further partial stadium closure.
The sanctions were imposed for ableist and homophobic chants, heard at a game against Charlton Athletic in January.
"These chants are discriminatory, unacceptable, and will not be tolerated at The Den or anywhere Millwall play," Millwall's managing director Mark Fairbrother said in an open letter to supporters. , external
"The club condemns them without reservation. They do not represent this club, and the vast majority of supporters who follow Millwall home and away with passion and pride.
"Incidents like this hurt all of us, but none more so than people who are directly discriminated against by ableist, homophobic or other unacceptable chanting, and we apologise to anybody that was affected, offended or impacted by the chants."
Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand - the two-tiered east stand at The Den - will have to be closed for the Championship fixture against Sheffield United on 8 December.
It is the first time a club has been given this level of sanction for discriminatory chanting, with the commission saying "the club's previous disciplinary record was a significant aggravating feature".
The commission pointed to chants relating to race in a 2019 fixture against Everton, religion in a 2023 fixture away at Wigan Athletic, and sexual orientation and disability in a 2025 visit to Crystal Palace, all of which resulted in fines for the club.
"History has shown that combinations of action plans and fines have been wholly ineffective to prevent the club - through its supporters - committing breaches" of Football Association (FA) rules around discriminatory behaviour, the commission added.
The FA had charged Millwall in March for the chanting against Charlton.
The club admitted the charge, and in its submissions suggested the chants were limited to 80 to 100 individuals in the north-eastern corner of the Dockers Stand, in the blocks that will be closed as part of the punishment.
However, based on other evidence, the commission concluded the actual figure involved in the chants was "likely to have been in the hundreds, quite possibly more".
It also found that the club did not make any announcement over the stadium PA system ordering for the discriminatory chanting to stop, nor did it deploy any additional stewards or police to the areas from where the chanting was originating.
"I won't dress this up. This is a serious outcome," Fairbrother said.
"This significant sanction was given because, although this is the first charge relating to a match at The Den for many years, the commission took into account a number of incidents of discriminatory chanting involving our supporters over the past few seasons at away games.
"This is the cumulative cost of that pattern. Most importantly, the current and any future sanctions mean the next incident won't just cost the club money. It will cost supporters their seats.
"Innocent fans will be shut out of their own stadium because of someone else's behaviour, and with future sanctions likely to be tougher, that threat is very real."

Freddie Potts has started all of Club Brugge's Champions League games
When Liverpool visit Club Brugge on Wednesday they are likely to come up against English midfielder Freddie Potts.
The 23-year-old ended a 16-year association with West Ham in the summer to join the Belgian champions for an undisclosed fee.
And he has started every game, bar one missed through suspension, in all competitions.
After losing to Aston Villa in the Champions League, they have defeated Inter Milan, Lens and PSV.
"It really is a dream because you hear the music and then you see your family in the stands and you remember all the times that you watched Champions League on TV," Potts told BBC Radio 5 Live's Euro Leagues Show.
"You think of all the memories that you make watching it and to be playing in it now is something that every kid dreams of."
Potts' whole life had been based around West Ham. He had been with the club since the age of six and his father Steve, who made 506 appearances for the Hammers, is a first-team coach.
Potts Jr played 28 times for West Ham, with 25 of them coming last season as they were relegated from the Premier League.
He also had loan spells with Wycombe in League One and Portsmouth in the Championship.
"In pre-season my minutes with West Ham were limited, they weren't as much as I wanted and then I spoke with my agent and said 'let's explore options because this season I'm 22, turning 23'," Potts said.
"It's a massive part of my career and I wanted to play. The opportunity of Club Brugge came along with Champions League football, the best club in Belgium and it was an opportunity I couldn't really turn down with how my minutes were going down with West Ham.
"I grew up in the area, going to the stadium watching the games. It was always going to be a tough decision but it was something that I had to do for my career.
"It was an emotional decision because it had to be made quite quickly. It's been the right decision for me and so far I'm enjoying it, I'm loving life here."
Club Brugge won the Belgian title last season and are second, just one point behind leaders Union Saint-Gilloise this campaign.
"It's a physical league," said Potts. "My running and physical stats have been higher than they've ever been. It's a demanding league in that way.
"Club Brugge demands a lot, from winning the ball back and going man for man in the press. And your responsibility off the ball is something that you have to take really seriously."
Freddie Potts on leaving West Ham, life in Belgium and beating Inter Milan
Potts says he has not started to learn French or Flemish and that team talks are done in English, with the side managed by Croat Ivan Leko.
"The whole move itself is funny because we used to visit Brugge when I was a kid," he said.
"We used to come around Christmas, so my family all know the city. And now I'm here they come out as much as they can.
"It's a great city with a lot of culture. It's brilliant. You won't find many places like it."
Next up for the side is the visit of Liverpool this week - with both clubs on nine points after four games.
"Everyone knows Liverpool as a club, the size and the Premier League teams," said Potts, who started for West Ham at home to the Reds last season.
"It's going to be a big game. We're level on points in the Champions League and we've put big performances in this competition and we're hoping that we're going to do the same."

Midfielder is preparing to face Liverpool after leaving the club he loves and overcoming a tough start in Belgium
I n April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions League seven months later.
It is the 23-year-old’s reward for taking the difficult decision to leave his boyhood club last summer. Potts noticed his minutes were drying up in pre-season, even though West Ham were not exactly stocked with talent after relegation, and he was ready for a new challenge when Club Brugge offered about £10m to sign him.
“I thought this was the perfect place for me to take the next step,” Potts says of his move to the Belgian champions. “I’m not going to shy away – it was very hard. West Ham have been my club for my whole life. I still have a lot of love for West Ham. But I had to take into account what was best for my career and I’m loving it at Brugge.
“Every player wants to be in the team expected to win every week, and seeing how Club Brugge have performed in the Champions League before shows the project and how they want to develop the team and players. It was a very exciting place for me to come. They look to develop young players.”
Potts was six when he joined West Ham. His father, Steve, made 506 appearances for the club and is part of Scott Parker’s backroom staff now. Freddie’s brother, Dan, came through the academy before moving to Luton in 2015. This is a West Ham family; it is no surprise that moving to Belgium was emotional for Potts.
Yet it was the right move. Brugge are second in the Belgian Pro League, a point behind Union Saint‑Gilloise, and have impressed in the Champions League. They have nine points from four games in the league phase and caused a stir when they beat Inter 4-3 at San Siro last month.
Potts calls it “one of the best nights of my career”. It was quite the turnaround for a player who mostly watched from the bench as West Ham tried to save themselves during the second half of last season. It helps that Potts knows how to stay calm. He was talked up as a future West Ham captain when he made his full debut and impressed in a 3-1 win over Newcastle last year. He had a run in the team but lost his place when Nuno switched to a 4-4-2 in January and settled on Mateus Fernandes and Tomas Soucek as his preferred partnership in central midfield.
That was when Potts remembered how he grew during loan spells at Portsmouth and Wycombe. “I know that you can have games where you feel like you are on top of the world, and then you can come straight back down,” he says. “The loans helped me out massively with West Ham because I managed to cope with the highs. The Newcastle game was a real high, but there were some lows after that and I feel like I was coping with it.”
Potts saw the reaction on social media when he left. Some West Ham fans were not happy with the club for allowing a homegrown player to depart. This season has been tough for West Ham, who are 10th in the Championship after a disappointing run and replaced Nuno with Parker this month. One problem has been the lack of a No 6. Potts, who can snap into a tackle and link play from deep, has been watching from afar.
“I still think they’re playing well,” he says. “They’ve got a great team, great players. I think Scott Parker is a really good manager and he’s got three teams promoted from the Championship. I don’t think it will be a problem again. West Ham will get promoted in the end.”
Potts has glitzier assignments and is adjusting to his surroundings. He cannot speak much Flemish but he has sipped a couple of Belgian beers and is enjoying life in Bruges. “I’m not going to lie, when I first joined I found it difficult. It’s completely different when you move country. But I was open to the challenge. At the start it was a challenge but now it’s really smooth.”
One of the biggest challenges has been adapting to a new style. Given the intensity of the Premier League it is a surprise to hear Potts say Brugge, managed by the 48-year‑old Croat Ivan Leko, have helped him become more physical.
“Straight away in training programmes it was a real surprise how hard everyone works,” Potts says. “It’s in the nature of the club to really work hard and give 100% every day. You see that straight away as you come in the door. No matter how hard it can be everyone gets on with it. No complaints. We’re a running team and everyone gives it their all. That’s the message from the top. It’s a real positive environment for someone of my age to be part of.”
Brugge have a couple of rising stars in attack: the rapid Portugal winger Carlos Forbs and the 22-year-old striker Nicolò Tresoldi, who scored a hat-trick in the win against Inter. There is a feeling Leko’s side could go on a run in Europe. They do not fear Liverpool. “It’ll be difficult for them coming to our place,” Potts says. “They’re a great team but we’re going to approach it like we have been doing with every game.
“Inter are one of the top teams in the competition. PSV are a great team and we got the win there. Liverpool will be tough but we’ve proved it against top teams before.”

League Two footballer Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged with rape.
Noel-Williams, who plays for League Two side Barnet, has been charged with three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault by penetration, Hertfordshire Police said.
The 23-year-old, of High Oaks, St Albans, was remanded in custody following a hearing at Hatfield Magistrates' Court on Saturday.
In a statement, the club said it was "co-operating fully with authorities" and would determine further action "in due course".
Noel-Williams has also been charged with one count of engaging in sexual communication with a child, and one count of supplying a controlled (Class B) drug, police added.
In a statement, the London club said: "Barnet FC can confirm that first-team player Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged and remanded in custody as part of a police investigation by Hertfordshire Constabulary.
"The club is co-operating fully with the authorities and will determine any further action in due course.
"As this is now a matter for the courts, the club will not be making any further comment."
Noel-Williams, who previously played for Hemel Hempstead Town, Kettering Town, Matlock Town, Harrow Borough and Cheshunt, joined Barnet in June.

Millwall have been punished for discriminatory chanting relating to disability and sexual orientation by fans in a game against Charlton in January; a two-game partial stadium closure (one game of which is suspended) is first of its kind at this level; Millwall also fined £70,000
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Millwall have become the first club in the top four divisions of English football to be punished with a partial stadium closure for discriminatory chanting after a regulatory commission proved two FA charges.
The unprecedented measure is for Millwall failing to ensure their supporters didn't engage in discriminatory chanting that includes reference to disability and sexual orientation during a home match with Charlton in January.
As well as a two-game partial stadium closure - one game of which is suspended until the end of the 2027/28 season - Millwall have been fined £70,000 plus hearing costs, warned about their future conduct, and have had their FA Action Plan extended until the end of next season.
Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand will be closed when Millwall host Sheffield United on December 8 - a total of 1,274 seats.
In their written conclusions, the commission found "the club's degree of culpability in relation to the incidents was significant".
In response, speaking exclusively to Sky Sports , Millwall managing director Mark Fairbrother said: "As a club, we didn't do enough and on behalf of the club I apologise to everyone who has been affected by that chanting because it shouldn't happen."
Millwall pleaded guilty to the charges but Fairbrother said Millwall were "disappointed" with the outcome.
He also pointed to new processes the club have since put in place to try to avoid a recurrence - but called on other football clubs, the FA, and organisations such as Kick It Out to come together to find preventative solutions.
"We challenge everything we do and look at if there are ways that we can improve? It's highlighted where we need to be better," he said. "We had already put mitigations in place and need to continue to do so.
"But this is one football club. These instances are happening across football. This is a challenge for the sport in general.
"We see it this [past] week with the charges to Chelsea and also the FA for the England fans in Spain . So, we can put measures in place but we're one club. We can't solve all of society's issues.
"We need to work with all key football stakeholders to look at how can we all do this better? What does good look like? What does best practice look like? And making sure that we embrace that. But everyone else has a collective responsibility as well."
Fairbrother says "the stick approach" used against clubs whose supporters are found guilty of discriminatory chanting just "punishes the fans who actually are just here to enjoy themselves". Instead, he asks "what can we do in terms of the carrot approach to educate people to eradicate this?"
He also noted that supporters identified in the discriminatory chanting against Charlton were all under 18 years old.
"That shows a lack of understanding of the implication of these words," he said. "These words obviously hurt and they have a significant impact on those groups that it affects. But there's that lack of understanding of the issue and the impact."
Asked if he would be interested in working more with groups such as Kick It Out to address this aspect, Fairbrother said: "I'd embrace it. From a personal perspective, I think that would be really good and I implore them to please come work with us, come and look at what we do, challenge what we do.
"If you don't think something we're doing is good enough, come and tell us but look at solutions. If we all have a solutions-focused mindset, we can actually start to make real difference."
The regulatory commission also wrote in their conclusions that "the reputation of the club and English football would have been tarnished" by the chanting during a game shown live on Sky Sports . Fairbrother feels that.
"It hurts all of us in the club. But I know it hurts our fans as well because that is not who we are," he said.
Millwall play Charlton again at the Den on December 19 in a Championship fixture. On how the club are working to avoid a repeat of the discriminatory chanting heard in January, Fairbrother said: "We've put in place a number of procedures already.
"We've already had West Ham here earlier in the season, which was probably our highest-risk fixture for a number of years. That went without incident. But we had a different approach to different fan groups in terms of just reminding them of their responsibility.
"But also for us as a club, making sure that we're on the front foot in terms of everything we do. We will have that same approach to Charlton. You can't predict the future, but we have a more robust process in place now."
This latest issue was the first case of discriminatory chanting at the Den since an FA Cup tie with Everton in 2019 - but follows three other cases involving Millwall supporters away from home since April 2023.
Asked whether he is confident of making a difference, Fairbrother said that would require the support of Millwall fans to call out discriminatory language.
"For each of those instances - and all three of them were away games - there were specific small fan groups who obviously engaged with that chanting. This is now the first instance we've had here at the Den," he said.
"So for all fans, we need to check and challenge this. We need to make sure it doesn't build up. Don't engage with this type of chanting.
"It's not fair on [other Millwall supporters]. We need to all do better. As a club, we need to do better and we will do better for them. But also, it's a collective one. If it happens, if people see it, call it out. We all need to be more proactive on this.
"I'm proud to represent Millwall and I think it goes against what this club's really about."
When contacted by Sky Sports News, Kick It Out said: "Kick It Out welcomes greater accountability for discriminatory mass chanting and supports greater collaboration between clubs and governing bodies to tackle this serious issue.
"Last season, we received a record number of mass chanting reports across football, including racist, sexist and misogynistic, homophobic, ableist and faith-based abuse. This is why we're conducting further research and campaigning to show its impact on communities and ensure more consistent action from clubs and authorities.
"Education has a key role here, both for fans, so that they know the impact and consequences of discriminatory chanting, and clubs, so they can proactively help to reduce its prevalence. We stand ready to support football in helping eradicate this problem."

Crystal Palace Women are being punished for making substitutions at four separate windows in a win over Everton in September - the last of which came in the 97th minute - which is in breach of IFAB Laws that state clubs have no more than three substitution opportunities in each match
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Crystal Palace Women have been deducted three points in the WSL with immediate effect.
Promoted side Palace, who now drop into the relegation play-off spot, are being punished for making substitutions at four separate windows in a 1-0 win over Everton in September.
This is in breach of IFAB Laws, which state clubs can make five substitutions, but have no more than three opportunities in each match to do so.
Palace made a substitution in a fourth window in the 97th minute of the match. Kirsty Howat, who was brought on for Shannon O'Brien, did not touch the ball before the full-time whistle was blown.
Palace admitted to the breach but felt the sanction sought by the WSL was "excessive", according to the written decisions published with the sanction.
However, the independent tribunal determined that a sporting sanction was necessary to avoid damaging the integrity of the competition.
In response, Palace said in a statement on Tuesday: "Everyone at the club is obviously frustrated that such a minor infraction, given that the player was on the pitch for only 46 seconds while the ball was in play, has led to such a significant penalty - a penalty which we do not agree is reasonable or proportionate.
"We are disappointed for the players and staff who worked so hard to secure a deserved victory on our return to the WSL."
Everton's points total is unaffected by the sanction. They remain 11th in the table on 12 points after 11 matches. Palace, meanwhile, drop to second bottom, falling behind Birmingham on goal difference.
Everton disagreed with the assertion of Palace head coach Jo Potter that the outcome of the match was unaffected by their use of a fourth substitution window.
In a letter to the independent tribunal, Everton set out a four-point argument for how the non-compliant substitution had a direct sporting impact on the match.
"Palace did not make an extra substitution but used an extra substitution window, making changes in the 63rd, 83rd, 90th and, crucially, the 97th minute.
"This is devastating for Palace because Kirsty Howat, who came on for Shannon O'Brien, was only on the pitch for a matter of seconds and she didn't touch the ball.
"It is recognised [by the independent tribunal] that this hasn't created any advantage for Palace when it comes to the result, they have to deter other teams from choosing not to adhere to this rule.
"This will be upsetting for Palace, who have dropped down to second bottom in the table. The team in 14th at bottom of the table, currently Charlton, will be immediately relegated.
"Whoever is 13th goes into a play-off against the winner of a match between the second and third team in WSL 2.
"This is gutting for Palace, who were above Birmingham before this deduction. Now they've dropped down and they're in danger. And, mentally, we know how hard it is for promoted teams to stay in the WSL."
